parts.title: Hiring a venue for a conference
parts.context: A woman phones a conference centre to ask about hiring a room.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman telephoning a conference centre to ask about hiring a venue. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Good morning, Harbour Point Conference Centre, Owen speaking.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Oh, good morning. I'm looking for somewhere to hold our annual conference. We're a small charity, so we have to watch the budget.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Of course. I'll take a few details, and then we can talk about what might suit you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The woman wants to hold a conference, so 'conference' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Right, could I take your name, please?

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Yes, it's Naomi Fenwick.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Sorry, could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Of course. It's F-E-N-W-I-C-K.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Thank you, Ms Fenwick. Now, which date did you have in mind?

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: We always hold it on a Friday, and this year we'd like the 5th of October, if that's free.
script.tts: We always hold it on a Friday, and this year we'd like the fifth of October, if that's free.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Ah, let me see. No, I'm afraid not. We've got a wedding fair that weekend. The following Friday, the 12th, is free, though.
script.tts: Ah, let me see. No, I'm afraid not. We've got a wedding fair that weekend. The following Friday, the twelfth, is free, though.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Yes, that would be fine. The 12th it is.
script.tts: Yes, that would be fine. The twelfth it is.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: And how many delegates are you expecting?

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Last year we had 40, but 52 people have already registered, and the form doesn't close for another month, so I'd say we should plan for 60.
script.tts: Last year we had forty, but fifty-two people have already registered, and the form doesn't close for another month, so I'd say we should plan for sixty.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Then I'd recommend the Atlantic Suite. It seats up to 80, with a stage at one end and moveable walls. The Lighthouse Room is cheaper, but it only holds 40.
script.tts: Then I'd recommend the Atlantic Suite. It seats up to eighty, with a stage at one end and moveable walls. The Lighthouse Room is cheaper, but it only holds forty.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Then the Atlantic Suite it is. Could we get in early to set up? The conference starts at ten, and registration opens at half past nine, but we'll have banners to put up.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Our cleaners finish at seven, so you could have the room from eight o'clock.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Eight is perfect, thank you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Now, is there anything special you'll need in the room?

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Yes. Our keynote speaker uses a wheelchair, so we'll need some way of getting her onto the stage.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: That's no problem. The building has a lift to every floor, but for the stage itself we have a portable ramp.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Thank you. And what about lunch?

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Yes, we can do either a sit-down meal or a buffet.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: A buffet will be fine. Most of us are vegetarian anyway, but one of our speakers has a serious reaction to nuts.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Vegetarian food is no problem. I'll let the chef know about the nuts.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Great. Now, what would the room cost?

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Um, the Atlantic Suite is 65 pounds an hour. Oh, no, sorry, I'm looking at the wrong line. That's the Lighthouse Room. For the Atlantic Suite it's 85 pounds an hour.
script.tts: Um, the Atlantic Suite is sixty-five pounds an hour. Oh, no, sorry, I'm looking at the wrong line. That's the Lighthouse Room. For the Atlantic Suite it's eighty-five pounds an hour.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: That's a little more than I'd hoped, but we'll manage. And when would you need an answer from us?

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Normally we ask for written confirmation and a deposit by the end of July. But since you're booking so early, we can stretch that to the end of August.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: That's very kind of you.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Would you like to come and look round the centre before you decide? We run tours on weekday afternoons.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Yes, I'd love to. Would Monday suit?

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Monday's no good, I'm afraid. We're closed for staff training. How about Tuesday?

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: I've got a meeting on Tuesday, I'm afraid. Could I come on Thursday instead?

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Thursday's fine. Shall we say two o'clock?

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Perfect. I'll see you then.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: I'll email you the details of everything we've discussed.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Thanks very much for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A library induction talk
parts.context: A librarian welcomes new students to a university library.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a librarian giving a talk to new students at a university library. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Dunmere University Library. My name's Helen, and I'm one of the subject librarians. I'll keep this short.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: First, opening hours. In term time we're open from eight until ten on weekdays. Many of you asked at the open day whether we could open earlier or close later, and I'm afraid the budget doesn't stretch to that. What we have managed to do is open on Sundays, from noon until six.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Now, borrowing. We used to charge twenty pence a day for overdue books, but we scrapped the fines two years ago. Now, if a book is overdue, your account is simply blocked, so you can't borrow anything else until it comes back. The only time money is involved is when a book is lost, and then you pay for a replacement.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Next, finding things. There's a booklet on referencing at the information desk, and subject librarians like me give one-to-one appointments, but those are mostly used by final-year students. What I'd really recommend is the workshop your department runs in week two. It's only an hour, and it shows you how to search for the sources you'll need for your first assignment.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Most of what you'll read is online, and you can reach it all from home. In the past you had to install special software on your laptop first, but you don't any more. You just log in on the library website with the same username and password you use for your university email.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: And if we haven't got a book you need, you can ask us to buy it. We used to have a suggestion book by the entrance, but hardly anyone used it, so it's been replaced by a form on the website. The staff at the desk can't place orders themselves, so there's no point asking them.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Now let me tell you about some of the spaces and services you'll be using. On the first floor there are twelve group study rooms, each with a screen and a whiteboard. They're very popular, so you can't just turn up and use one. You need to book a slot online, for up to two hours at a time.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: On the third floor you'll find the research carrels, but those are reserved for postgraduates, I'm afraid, so they're out of bounds for you for now.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Down in the basement is the computer suite, with a hundred and fifty computers and all the specialist software for your courses. The rest of the building closes at ten, but the suite has its own entrance, and it's open day and night, every day of the year.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Now, a place you might not expect: our Special Collections room, on the ground floor, where we keep rare books, old maps and letters, some of them four hundred years old. Anyone can go in, you just sign in at the door. But nothing may leave the room, not even for an hour.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Next to the café, which is being doubled in size next year, is the Digital Lab. It has 3D printers, a scanner and video-editing equipment, all free to use. But before you touch any of it, you have to attend a short training session, so that nobody gets hurt and nothing gets broken.
script.tts: Next to the café, which is being doubled in size next year, is the Digital Lab. It has three-D printers, a scanner and video-editing equipment, all free to use. But before you touch any of it, you have to attend a short training session, so that nobody gets hurt and nothing gets broken.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Finally, if we don't have a book, we can often borrow it from another university. That's called an inter-library loan. Ordinary borrowing is free, but this service costs three pounds per item, which covers the postage.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: That's all from me. Thank you, and enjoy your first term.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A river water-quality experiment
parts.context: Two environmental science students discuss their river experiment with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Maya and Tom, discussing an experiment on river water quality with their tutor, Dr Hale. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Come in, you two. First of all, remind me why you chose the River Linnet. I seem to remember you considering the Dene as well.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: We did. The Dene's nearer, but it only has one easy place to reach the water. The Linnet has public footpaths along both banks, so we could sample above and below the sewage works at Thornby.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: The council's old tests were no use, because their records stop in 2015.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Fair enough. And your methods? You planned to use the chemical test kit for dissolved oxygen.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: We did start with that, but the colour changes were really hard to judge, so the department lent us an electronic probe instead.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: The nitrate samples we took back to the lab, though.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Good. Any problems on the days themselves?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Not with the equipment, and the farmer at the first site was happy for us to cross his field. The real problem was the weather. It had rained heavily the night before our second visit, and the river was much higher and browner, so the readings weren't comparable.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: So we went back three days later.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Sensible. And the nitrate results?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: That's the surprising bit. We expected the highest level just below the sewage works, and none of the sites went over the legal limit. But the highest reading was upstream, at the first site, where the river runs through farmland.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: That's not as odd as you might think. Fertiliser washes off fields all the time. And the invertebrates?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: We held the same net in the water for three minutes at each site, and counted the mayfly larvae and the other creatures. A technician at the museum checked what we'd identified.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Good. But I'm a bit worried about the numbers. One three-minute sweep at each site is a very small sample, so I'd be cautious about relying on them.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Right, now the report. I'd like a map showing your three sites and the land around them.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: I'd also like a short section about the rain. Explain what happened on your second visit and how you dealt with it.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Should we put all the raw data in the main text? There's an awful lot of it.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: No, that goes in an appendix.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: What about comparing our results with the council's old records, or listing every possible source of pollution?

script.speaker: hale
script.text: I wouldn't bother with either. The records are too old, and a list would be more than you need.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: OK. So our conclusion will be that farming has a bigger effect on the river than the sewage works.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: I'd be careful about that. Your results certainly point that way, but I'd say they're consistent with the idea, rather than proof of it.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: For the results section, I thought a map with coloured circles for each site might look good.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: It might, but circles are hard to compare. I'd go for a separate bar chart for each measurement. One big graph with everything on it would be far too crowded.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Now, one more thing that would strengthen your argument. The Environment Agency publishes monthly nitrate figures for the Linnet. If you ask for the same weeks, you could see whether your readings are typical.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Should we go back to the river this weekend and take more samples?

script.speaker: hale
script.text: No, you've got enough. Use the time to start writing.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: OK. We'll email the Agency this afternoon, then, and start on the introduction tomorrow.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how volcanic islands form
parts.context: A lecture about how volcanic islands are formed.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how volcanic islands form. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at how volcanic islands are formed. Some islands, like Britain, are simply pieces of continent that were cut off when the sea level rose. Volcanic islands are quite different, because they are built from nothing, one eruption at a time, starting on the sea floor, sometimes several kilometres below the surface.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Broadly speaking, there are two situations in which this happens. The first is at the boundary between two tectonic plates, where one plate is forced down beneath the other. As the sinking plate descends into the hot mantle, it carries water down with it, trapped in the rocks of the sea floor.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: You might expect heat alone to make the rock melt, but in fact it's the water that does it, because it lowers the melting point of the rock above. The molten rock, or magma, then rises and breaks through the sea floor. Since the boundary is usually curved, the volcanoes appear along a curve, and the islands they build are known as an island arc. Japan is the best-known example.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The second situation is the one I find more interesting. Here, the islands are nowhere near a plate boundary, but in the middle of a plate. The explanation is what we call a hotspot. Deep inside the Earth, a narrow column of extremely hot rock rises slowly towards the surface. Geologists call this a plume. When the plume reaches the base of the plate, it melts the rock, and the magma pushes its way upwards and erupts.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The best example is Hawaii, in the middle of the Pacific. The hotspot stays in more or less the same place, but the plate above it is moving, at roughly the speed your fingernails grow, about eight centimetres a year. So each volcano is carried away from the hotspot and slowly dies, while a new one begins to form over it. Over millions of years, this produces a chain of islands.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: That means we can tell the age of each island from its position. The island furthest from the hotspot is the oldest, while the youngest is the one sitting right above it, which in Hawaii is the Big Island.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Now let's follow the life of a single hotspot island. It begins with an eruption on the sea floor, perhaps four or five kilometres down. When the hot lava meets the cold water, it cools almost immediately and forms rounded shapes that look like cushions, which is why geologists call it pillow lava.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Eruption after eruption, these pillows pile up, and over several hundred thousand years they build an enormous underwater volcano, known as a seamount.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Eventually, the top of the seamount breaks the surface, and a new island is born. But its troubles begin straight away, because waves, wind and rain start to wear it down. This process is called erosion, and it never stops.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Meanwhile, the moving plate is carrying the island away from the hotspot. Once it has moved too far, the supply of magma is cut off, and the volcano stops erupting for good. We say that it has become extinct. Without new lava to replace what the sea removes, the island starts to shrink.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: There's a second problem. As the plate moves away from the hotspot, it cools, and cool rock is heavier, so the whole island slowly sinks. But in warm tropical water, corals grow around the edge of the island, forming a reef. As the island sinks, the corals keep growing upwards towards the light, and in the end the volcano disappears altogether, leaving only a ring of coral around a lagoon. This is called an atoll.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: It was Charles Darwin who first suggested this idea, in the 1830s, but nobody could prove it until drilling in the 1950s found volcanic rock deep beneath the coral.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So, to sum up, a volcanic island is born, grows, shrinks and finally vanishes, and the whole cycle can take tens of millions of years. Next week, we'll look at the plants and animals that colonise these islands. Thank you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write **ONE WORD ONLY** for each answer.
groups.title: Volcanic islands
content: ## Plate boundaries
• one plate sinks below another and takes {{31}} down with it, which makes the rock above melt
• magma breaks through the sea floor, building a curved group of islands called an island {{32}}
## Hotspots
• a thin stream of extremely hot rock, called a {{33}}, rises from deep within the Earth
• the plate moves slowly across the hotspot, so a {{34}} of islands results
• the oldest island is the one {{35}} from the hotspot

questions.explanation: The sinking plate ‘carries water down with it’, and it is the water, not the heat, that lowers the melting point of the rock above.
questions.cue: it carries water down with it

questions.explanation: Because the boundary is curved, the islands ‘are known as an island arc’.
questions.cue: are known as an island arc

questions.explanation: ‘Deep inside the Earth, a narrow column of extremely hot rock rises’; the lecturer says ‘Geologists call this a plume’.
questions.cue: Geologists call this a plume

questions.explanation: As the plate moves over the fixed hotspot, ‘this produces a chain of islands’.
questions.cue: this produces a chain of islands

questions.explanation: Islands can be dated by position: ‘The island furthest from the hotspot is the oldest’, while the youngest sits right above it.
questions.cue: The island furthest from the hotspot is the oldest

groups.instruction: Complete the flow-chart below. Write **ONE WORD ONLY** for each answer.
groups.title: Life cycle of a hotspot island
content: Lava meets cold water on the sea floor, cools rapidly and forms rounded shapes known as {{36}} lava.
Over hundreds of thousands of years, repeated eruptions build an underwater volcano called a {{37}}.
Once the island appears, waves, wind and rain gradually wear it down in a process called {{38}}.
The moving plate carries the island away from the hotspot, so the volcano stops erupting and becomes {{39}}.
The island sinks as the rock cools, and eventually only a ring of coral is left, called an {{40}}.

questions.explanation: Lava cooled at once by cold water forms rounded shapes like cushions, ‘which is why geologists call it pillow lava’.
questions.cue: which is why geologists call it pillow lava

questions.explanation: The piled-up pillows build an enormous underwater volcano, ‘known as a seamount’.
questions.cue: known as a seamount

questions.explanation: Once the island appears, waves, wind and rain wear it down: ‘This process is called erosion’.
questions.cue: This process is called erosion

questions.explanation: When the island has moved too far from the hotspot, the magma supply is cut off: ‘We say that it has become extinct’.
questions.cue: We say that it has become extinct

questions.explanation: The island sinks while coral keeps growing upwards, leaving a ring of coral around a lagoon: ‘This is called an atoll’.
questions.cue: This is called an atoll
